extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and professional authors (novelists and travel writers), editors and publishers interested in authorial craft and publication practice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical guidance for writing, publishing, and presenting fiction and nonfiction (novels, serialized stories, and travel books): discipline, audience-awareness, handling sensitive subjects, length/format decisions, and research/readability standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuality and professional industry
rubrics_metrics.description: An author who writes for these publications is bound to suit himself to these exigencies; with all the pages that I have written for magazines I have never been a day late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep to agreed deadlines and quantities; sit down to work at a certain hour; do not rely on 'inspiration' as an excuse for irregularity; punctual authors should not assume exemption from ordinary business bonds. Be mindful that others' irregularity may still harm you, but maintain personal regularity to avoid causing inconvenience to editors, publishers, and printers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect publishing schedules and serialization exigencies
rubrics_metrics.description: An author who writes for these publications is bound to suit himself to these exigencies, and can generally do so without personal loss or inconvenience, if he will only take time by the forelock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan manuscripts to fit magazine dates and editorial timetables; when magazines change plans (e.g., Victor Hugo causing scheduling conflict), be prepared to negotiate alternatives (separate numbers, other periodicals) but aim to conform to the periodical's schedule whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting output and setting quotas (methodical composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word was counted... I have always succeeded in getting a desk put up in my cabin, and this was done ready for me in the Great Britain, so that I could go to work the day after we left Liverpool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, measurable production quotas (words/pages per day or week — e.g., 66 manuscript pages per week at 250 words per page). Keep track of supplied vs. contracted matter to avoid shortfalls that force filling or cause dispute with printers/editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain readable length and avoid unnecessary stretching
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all the needs a book has the chief need is that it be readable... I had settled with my conscience to be the proper length of a novel volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an appropriate, readable length (author cites ~300 pages with ~220 words/page as proper). Resist publishers' attempts to split/expand work into extra volumes purely for packaging reasons, because this can hurt readers (additional cost, inconvenience) and the work's readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate format/volume decisions to protect readers' interests
rubrics_metrics.description: When it had passed through the magazine, the subsequent use of it was sold to other publishers ... it was to be brought out by them as a novel in two volumes. Now it had been sold by me as a novel in one volume, and hence there arose a correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author should assert reasonable objections to format changes that disadvantage readers or change intended presentation (e.g., two volumes vs. one). Be aware publishers may prioritize commercial/formatting aims; stand to protect the reader and the integrity of the book when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth to life; avoid pretension and un-natural portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: I regard [Victor Hugo's latter novels] as pretentious and untrue to nature... To write in fiction of one so fallen as the noblest of her sex, as one to be rewarded because of her weakness, as one whose life is happy, bright, and glorious, is certainly to allure to vice and misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle characters and incidents realistically; avoid romanticizing or portraying implausible, glamorized outcomes for morally fraught characters. Truthful depiction serves moral and artistic purposes and avoids misleading impressionable readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposeful handling of sensitive subjects (e.g., 'fallen women')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vicar of Bullhampton was written chiefly with the object of exciting not only pity but sympathy for a fallen woman, and of raising a feeling of forgiveness for such in the minds of other women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about authorial intent when addressing delicate moral/social issues (prefaces can be used). If the aim is reforming readers' attitudes (sympathy, forgiveness), structure narrative and characterization to support that pedagogical or moral purpose rather than titillation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glamorizing vice; depict consequences honestly
rubrics_metrics.description: There is seen a false glitter of gaudy life... which, alas! has been more often portrayed in glowing colours, for the injury of young girls, than have those horrors which ought to deter...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting vice, show its real consequences — squalor, disease, hunger, degradation — rather than focusing on superficial allurements. This discourages imitation and offers an honest deterrent; punitive 'houses of refuge' should also avoid merely austere punishments that fail to rehabilitate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and prominence of morally sensitive characters
rubrics_metrics.description: I could not venture to make this female the heroine of my story. To have made her a heroine at all would have been directly opposed to my purpose. It was necessary therefore that she should be a second-rate personage in the tale;--but it was with reference to her life that the tale was written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a problematic character should be central or secondary based on the story's objective: make them subordinate if the aim is to use their condition to illuminate social attitudes rather than to celebrate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience suitability and protecting young readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a novelist, who professes to write for the amusement of the young of both sexes, should allow himself to bring upon his stage a character such as that of Carry Brattle... Cannot women, who are good, pity the sufferings of the vicious, and do something perhaps to mitigate and shorten them without contamination from the vice?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the composition and sensibilities of your intended audience (including young readers) when deciding what to depict. If including disturbing material, handle it in a way that informs or prompts sympathy in mature readers while minimizing corrupting influence on youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of preface to state moral or artistic aims
rubrics_metrics.description: To this novel I affixed a preface,--in doing which I was acting in defiance of my old-established principle. I do not know that any one read it; but as I wish to have it read, I will insert it here again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preface can be used to explain the author's aim (e.g., to elicit sympathy rather than sensationalize); this can frame readers' interpretations and justify unconventional choices in portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research, immersion and honesty in nonfiction/travel writing
rubrics_metrics.description: I visited them all... I was absent in all eighteen months, and think that I did succeed in learning much of the political, social, and material condition of these countries... I thoroughly imbued my mind with the subject, and wrote with the simple intention of giving trustworthy information on the state of the Colonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For informative travel or country studies, undertake thorough first-hand inquiry, visit relevant regions, listen, and record observations. Strive for honest reporting and acknowledge possible inaccuracies due to speed of work, but labour to make the account trustworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability as primary criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all the needs a book has the chief need is that it be readable. Feeling that these volumes on Australia were dull and long, I was surprised to find that they had an extensive sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize readability over exhaustive completeness or purely scholarly detail; even honest, well-researched books fail without readable style. If pages 'drag', the work will fail to engage most readers regardless of authorial affection for the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone to audience and purpose (lightness for accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a work, unless it be light, cannot answer the purpose for which it is intended. It was not exactly a school-book that was wanted, but something that would carry the purposes of the school-room even into the leisure hours of adult pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing explanatory or classical material for general readers (e.g., 'Ancient Classics for English Readers'), adopt a light, accessible tone rather than heavy pedantry to reach the intended audience and make learning pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding gratuitous detail that distracts from main purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: I have not introduced her lover on the scene, nor have I presented her to the reader in the temporary enjoyment of any of those fallacious luxuries, the longing for which is sometimes more seductive to evil than love itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit incidental glamour or sensational detail if it would undermine the moral or thematic point. Keep secondary luxuries or temptations out of scenes where they would distract from the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial realism about remuneration and genre choice
rubrics_metrics.description: For such a work as this I had always been aware that I could not fairly demand more than half the price that would be given for the same amount of fiction... travelling with the object of writing is not a good trade. If the travelling author can pay his bills, he must be a good manager on the road.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic about the market value of different types of writing (travel books often pay less than fiction); budget and manage costs accordingly; understand the commercial incentives shaping publisher offers and plan work/finances prudently.
